newsitem.title: UK: Colombia plans further structural reforms - FinMin.
newsitem.headline: Colombia plans further structural reforms - FinMin.

text.p: Colombia's government plans to implement further structural reforms in the second half of this year, its finance minister said in an interview on Friday.
"More structural reforms will be undertaken, mainly for reducing transfers (to municipalities) and reforming the social security system," Jose Antonio Ocampo told Reuters.
The central government funds education and health spending by Colombian states and municipalities receive money for general investment purposes.

"The main rise (in transfers) is due to increases to municipalities, which has to be done under existing legislation. We are discussing ways of slowing down the rate of increase. It will be looked at in the second semester," Ocampo said.

Reforms to Colombia's social security system would focus on pension fund changes. The government might change the pensionable age and also implement stronger rules for transfers between private and public pension funds, Ocampo said.
"We have not taken any final decisions yet. As private and public pension funds now stand, there could be a small deficit."
Ocampo was in London to meet investors ahead of a $750 million 10-year bond issue due next week.
In January, Colombia introduced an emergency package of austerity measures to curb the country's high deficit and to reduce the heavy inflow of dollars.
The main points included cuts in expenditure, a reduction in public sector indebtedness abroad, a temporary tax on foreign debt and a crack-down on tax evasion.
The peso has fallen sharply since then and interest rates have also declined. Ocampo said he hoped central bank rates would fall by another two to three percentage points this month.

The measures have led to increased social unrest, with at least 800,000 public employees planning to strike on February 11 in protest of below-inflation wage rises and the threat some nationalised industries may be privatised.
The central government's deficit before privatisation revenues was 4.0 percent in 1996, and the government planned to reduce it to 3.2 percent this year, Ocampo said.
The economy's growth target was 4.0 to 4.5 percent and inflation was aimed at 18 percent.
"The market has had a very positive reaction, first to the law which let the government take properties of drug traffickers last year and then to the austerity package," Ocampo said.
Colombia planned to borrow between $1.4 billion and $1.5 billion in the international capital markets in 1997.
